fields.title: How to Ask Questions Without Getting Polite Lies
fields.keyTakeaway: Ask about what the person has already done in a specific recent case. Anything they say about the future or what they “usually” do is a forecast and self-description, not data.
fields.checkQuestion: Why is “would you use a report like this?” worse than “how did you do this last month?”
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node is the same — **how to ask questions** — but here it is about form. People want to be helpful and polite. To the question “would that be convenient for you?”, almost everyone answers “yes”, and that means nothing.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you ignore this.** Ten interviews confirm the idea, the feature is launched, and no one uses it. The research wasn't wrong — it measured politeness.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Four rules that are enough for your first year
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **About the past, not the future.** “What did you do when...” instead of “what would you do if...”.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **About a specific case, not usually.** “Last Tuesday” instead of “as a rule”.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Without leading the answer.** Do not name the option you want to hear — it will be handed right back to you.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Stay silent after the answer.** The most valuable part usually comes after a three-second pause.
fields.blocks/3/items/0: “Do you need shift swap notifications?” → “How did you find out that the swap was confirmed last time?”
fields.blocks/3/items/1: “How often do you usually edit the schedule?” → “When was the last time you edited the schedule, and what happened then?”
fields.blocks/3/items/2: “Is it convenient for you to work with a spreadsheet?” → “Show me how you did it last month.”
fields.blocks/3/items/3: “Would you pay for a feature like this?” → “What are you buying or doing manually right now to cover this?”
fields.blocks/4/text:
Question: “Would it be useful for you to see monthly hours for everyone?” — “Yes, of course, useful.”
Question: “Show me how you calculated hours last month.” — The person opens a spreadsheet with three sheets and a formula, explaining along the way that they made a mistake once.

The first answer cannot be used. The second one is the real insight.
fields.blocks/4/title: Smena, two answers to the same core question
fields.blocks/5/text: Past behavior does not predict the reaction to something that does not exist yet. If a product changes the task itself rather than speeding up an existing one, the interview will only show the current workaround — after that, you need a prototype or an experiment, not a conversation.
